reason: In src/git-auth.ts:8, `gitAuthArgs` decides whether to attach the service token with `remoteUrl.includes("github.com")`. That is a substring test, not a check of the parsed hostname. URLs such as `https://github.com.evil.example/x.git` or `https://evil.example/github.com/x.git` pass it, and the function returns `-c http.extraHeader=Authorization: Bearer <token>`. In src/worktree.ts:15, `cloneRepo` passes that header together with SERVICE_TOKEN (HARBOR_GITHUB_TOKEN, from src/config.ts:4) to `git clone` for the same URL. Git then sends the header to whatever host the URL names. The URL comes from user input: in src/routes.ts:19-22, `registerRepo` takes `remoteUrl` from `req.body`, checks only that it is non-empty, and calls `cloneRepo` with it. No code on this path parses the URL or allowlists the host. Both member locations are real parts of this one defect.

evidence.code: export const SERVICE_TOKEN = process.env.HARBOR_GITHUB_TOKEN ?? "";

failure_scenario: An authenticated user calls registerRepo with body {id: "x", remoteUrl: "https://github.com.attacker.example/r.git"}. The route checks only that remoteUrl is non-empty and calls cloneRepo. gitAuthArgs sees the "github.com" substring and returns the bearer header. `git clone` then sends its HTTP request to github.com.attacker.example with `Authorization: Bearer <HARBOR_GITHUB_TOKEN>`. The attacker's server logs the header and now holds the service's GitHub token.
severity_reason: This is a secret leak that any user who can register a repository can exploit. It needs one request with a URL of the attacker's choosing, and it exposes the service-wide GitHub token, which gives access to every repository that token can reach.

reason: In src/api.ts, `json()` (line 7) throws on any non-2xx status. `fetchCurrentUser` (line 13) returns that promise without a catch, and `loadDashboard` awaits it at line 27 with no try/catch. The only caller, `mountDashboard` in src/dashboard.ts:5, calls `void loadDashboard(...)`. It attaches no `.catch` and shows no error UI, so any rejection is dropped. The root element keeps showing "Loading..." and `render` is never called. The issue is confirmed at src/api.ts:13 and src/api.ts:27. One part of F03 is wrong: `fetchUserList` (lines 16-24) cannot reject. It returns [] when `!res.ok` and has a catch-all that returns [], so only `fetchCurrentUser` can make the dashboard load fail. F03's main defect, an unhandled rejection in loadDashboard that stops the render, still holds, so it is on topic.
failure_scenario: A user's session expires and GET /api/me returns 401, or the request fails with a network error. `json()` throws `HTTP 401`, so `fetchCurrentUser` rejects and `loadDashboard` rejects at src/api.ts:27 before it calls `render`. `mountDashboard` discards the promise with `void`. The page stays on "Loading..." with no error message and no retry, and the browser logs an unhandled promise rejection.
severity_reason: The bug only shows up when /api/me fails, such as an expired session, a server error or a network drop. That is an error path, not the normal load path. When it happens, the dashboard hangs on "Loading..." with no feedback to the user. Nothing is corrupted and there is no security impact, so this is wrong behavior on an edge case, not on a common path.

reason: No code checks repository ids anywhere in the repo. In src/routes.ts, registerRepo (lines 19-22) only checks that id is non-empty. It stores the id and calls cloneRepo, and cloneRepo in src/worktree.ts uses cachePath(id) = path.resolve(REPOS_DIR, id) as the clone destination. template (line 36) builds base = path.join(REPOS_DIR, req.params.id). Its startsWith(base) check on line 38 only keeps the file inside base, and the caller controls base, so a traversing id defeats the check. cacheListing (lines 60-61) reads path.resolve(REPOS_DIR, id)/INDEX. path.resolve with an absolute id like "/etc" ignores REPOS_DIR, and "../.." segments walk out of it. Store.insertRepo only runs a parameterized INSERT. config.ts sets REPOS_DIR to "/var/harbor/repos" and does no filtering. CLAUDE.md, which F14 cites, is not in the working tree. F14's claim does not depend on it, though: the template route really does use the raw id.
failure_scenario: A user posts registerRepo with body id "../../../tmp/evil". cloneRepo then runs git clone into /tmp/evil, outside /var/harbor/repos. On the template route, id "../../.." (for example, sent URL-encoded) makes base "/". A name of "../etc/passwd" then resolves to /etc/passwd, which passes the startsWith("/") check, and the file is returned. cacheListing with id "/etc" reads /etc/INDEX, and with id ".." it reads /var/harbor/INDEX.
severity_reason: The template route can read any file the process can read, and registerRepo can clone into any writable directory, so this is a real path traversal. How much of it can be exploited through URL params depends on how the router, which is not in the repo, decodes slashes. The body-supplied id in registerRepo is not limited by that. I rated it High rather than Critical because of that uncertainty.

reason: In src/store.ts, Store.deleteRepo runs an unconditional delete only when ctx.isAdmin is true. For everyone else it runs line 29: `DELETE FROM repos WHERE id = ? AND (owner = ? OR owner = 'system')`. The `OR owner = 'system'` clause means a non-admin's delete also matches any repo owned by 'system', not just the caller's own repos. The route handler in src/routes.ts (deleteRepo, line 28) passes req.params.id and req.user straight to store.deleteRepo and does no ownership check of its own. I searched the tree for other guards and found none: nothing else references 'system' or isAdmin, there are no tests, and there is no middleware that limits this route to admins. The only admin-style check in routes.ts is isAdminAddress, and it applies only to auditLog. Both findings describe this same defect, one at the call site and one at the SQL filter.
failure_scenario: A repo row exists with id 'shared-infra' and owner 'system'. Any logged-in non-admin user (for example oid 'alice', isAdmin false) calls the deleteRepo route with params.id = 'shared-infra'. The route calls Store.deleteRepo, which runs `DELETE FROM repos WHERE id = 'shared-infra' AND (owner = 'alice' OR owner = 'system')`. The row matches the owner = 'system' branch, so the delete succeeds and returns 204. A shared system repository is gone for every user.
severity_reason: This is an authorization bypass that any authenticated user can trigger with one request. It permanently deletes shared, system-owned repository records, which is data loss affecting all users. The attacker only needs the repo id, and no admin rights or unusual state are required.

reason: The claim does not match the code. `fetchUserList` in src/api.ts (lines 16-24) does not throw on a non-2xx response. Line 19 checks `res.ok` and returns an empty array when the status is not 2xx. The whole body is also inside a try/catch (lines 17 and 21-23) that returns `[]` for network errors and JSON parse errors. It does not use the throwing `json<T>` helper (line 7). An expired session that makes /api/admin/users return 401 or 403 therefore gives an empty user list, and nothing propagates to `loadDashboard`. The only function in this file that throws on a non-2xx response is `fetchCurrentUser`, through `json()`. That is a different function, and the finding does not describe it.
severity_reason: There is no defect. On a non-2xx response or an exception, `fetchUserList` returns an empty array instead of throwing.

reason: In src/ci.ts:4, getBuild calls `fetch(`${CI}/builds/${id}`)` with no options: no `signal`, no AbortController, and no AbortSignal.timeout. I searched src/ for timeout, setTimeout, signal and server/listen setup and found none. The only caller, the `build` route in src/routes.ts:52, awaits getBuild directly with no timeout or race. Nothing in the repository limits how long this outbound request can take. One mitigation applies: on Node, the built-in fetch (undici) has default headers and body timeouts of about 300 seconds. So under Node the request fails after about five minutes instead of hanging forever. That lowers the impact, but the claim stands: the code sets no timeout of its own, and a stalled CI endpoint holds every /build request open for minutes. On a runtime without those defaults, it can hold them open with no limit.

evidence.code: no matches: no timeout or abort signal is configured anywhere in src/

failure_scenario: ci.example.com accepts the TCP connection but stops responding. Each request to the `build` route (src/routes.ts:52) then waits inside getBuild's fetch (src/ci.ts:4). On Node that wait lasts until undici's roughly 300-second default timeout. On other runtimes it may never end. While the CI server stays stalled, callers pile up with open requests and held resources, and none of them gets a timely error.
severity_reason: This is a real reliability risk, but it only shows up when the external CI service stalls. On Node, undici's default timeouts of about 300 seconds limit the wait, so it is not an unbounded hang or an outage in normal use. That fits Medium better than High.

reason: In src/config.ts, line 3 sets ADMIN_CIDR = "0.0.0.0/0", and isAdminAddress (line 6) calls cidrContains with that value. In cidrContains (line 12), a prefix length of 0 makes mask = 0. Line 13 then computes (toInt(base) & 0) === (toInt(ip) & 0), which is 0 === 0, so it returns true for every input. That includes non-IPv4 strings such as IPv6 addresses: toInt returns NaN for them, and NaN & 0 is 0. The only access control in routes.ts auditLog (line 43) is `if (!isAdminAddress(req.ip)) return { status: 403 }`. That check can never fail, so the handler always reads and returns AUDIT_LOG. auditLog does not check req.user or any role, and I found no other guard in the repo. I could not see how buildRoutes is mounted or whether some upstream auth exists, because nothing in the repo mounts it. Even so, the IP allowlist, which is the handler's only admin check, is a no-op as written.

evidence.code: export const ADMIN_CIDR = "0.0.0.0/0";

failure_scenario: A client from any address, for example req.ip = "203.0.113.7" from the public internet, calls the auditLog route. isAdminAddress("203.0.113.7") computes mask 0, so (0 & 0) === (anything & 0) and it returns true. The 403 branch is skipped, and the handler returns the full contents of /var/harbor/audit.log with status 200. Non-admin callers can read the audit log.
severity_reason: The only admin check on auditLog (src/routes.ts:43) always passes, so any caller that reaches the route gets the sensitive audit log. I rated this High, not Critical, because the repo does not show how the routes are mounted or whether some upstream authentication limits who can reach them.

reason: The claim holds. The working tree has 13 files: package.json and 12 files in src/, with no test or spec files anywhere. package.json defines "test": "node --test", but that command finds no test files, so nothing checks src/crypto.ts. Nothing tests that encrypt() output can be decrypted back to the original text (the round trip), and nothing tests that decrypt() rejects a changed ciphertext or auth tag (tamper detection). One weak point is left unchecked: decrypt() (src/crypto.ts:10-15) splits the sealed string and passes the tag to setAuthTag with no check on its length, and no authTagLength is set on createDecipheriv. A tamper test is the kind of test that would find this. Neither encrypt nor decrypt is called anywhere else in src/, so the missing tests are a quality and reliability gap, not a failure on a live code path.

evidence.code: "scripts": { "build": "tsc -p .", "test": "node --test" }

evidence.location: file listing (find . -type f): no test files
evidence.code: ./package.json ./src/routes.ts ./src/jira.ts ./src/worktree.ts ./src/crypto.ts ./src/git-auth.ts ./src/api.ts ./src/dashboard.ts ./src/untracked.ts ./src/ci.ts ./src/config.ts ./src/tasks.ts ./src/store.ts

failure_scenario: Someone changes encrypt() or decrypt() in src/crypto.ts, for example the token order or encoding, or how the auth tag is handled. Data sealed by encrypt() then no longer decrypts, or decrypt() accepts a shortened or altered auth tag. Running npm test ("node --test") still passes because there are no test files, so the regression ships without notice.
severity_reason: This is missing test coverage, not wrong behavior in the code now. encrypt and decrypt are not called anywhere else in the repository. Leaving authenticated-encryption code untested is still a significant reliability and security-maintenance risk, so Medium fits better than the High the review assigned.

reason: In src/jira.ts:4, getIssue calls `fetch(`${JIRA}/issue/${key}`)` with no options at all: no `signal`, no AbortSignal.timeout, and no AbortController. Its only caller, the `issue` route handler in src/routes.ts:48, awaits it directly and adds no timeout either. The repository sets no global dispatcher or agent timeout anywhere (a grep for timeout, AbortSignal, setGlobalDispatcher and undici finds nothing), and package.json has no HTTP client dependency. So the only limits are Node's built-in undici defaults: about 10s to connect, and about 300s each for headers and for body idle time. A Jira server that accepts the connection but responds slowly or stalls keeps each issue request pending for up to roughly five minutes, possibly longer if it trickles the body. `res.json()` has no bound either. The review's wording "hangs every caller" is a little too strong, because the wait is bounded by undici's defaults and does not block the event loop. The main defect is real, though: the app sets no timeout of its own. searchAssigned (line 10) has the same pattern.

evidence.location: package.json (full file; no HTTP client deps, no timeout config)
evidence.code: "scripts": { "build": "tsc -p .", "test": "node --test" }

failure_scenario: Jira at jira.example.com accepts TCP connections but stops responding, for example because it is overloaded or a proxy is holding requests. Every request to the `issue` route (src/routes.ts:48) awaits getIssue's fetch at src/jira.ts:4, which has no abort signal. Each client waits up to about 300 seconds, undici's default headers timeout, before getting an error. Meanwhile the pending requests and their sockets pile up in the server instead of failing fast.
severity_reason: This is a reliability risk that only shows up when the Jira dependency is degraded. Node's fetch still enforces default connect, headers and body timeouts of about 10s and 300s, so requests do not hang forever and the event loop is not blocked. That makes it less serious than an outage on a common path.

reason: In src/jira.ts:9, `searchAssigned` builds the JQL as `assignee = "${email}" ORDER BY created DESC` with no escaping. Line 10 applies `encodeURIComponent` to the whole JQL string. That only encodes it for the URL; it does not escape `"` or `\` inside the JQL. The only caller, `assignedIssues` in src/routes.ts:56, passes `req.body.email` straight in, and nothing in between validates or sanitizes it. The `Request.body` type is just `Record<string, string>`. A request body value containing `"` therefore ends the string literal and adds arbitrary JQL clauses. Nothing in the repo prevents this. The impact is limited, though. The fetch sends no credentials, and the route already lets the caller pick any email. `getIssue` also accepts any issue key. So the injection widens which query is run, but it does not clearly cross a privilege boundary that is visible in this code.
failure_scenario: A client calls the assignedIssues route with body email = `x" OR project = SECRET OR assignee = "y`. `searchAssigned` builds `assignee = "x" OR project = SECRET OR assignee = "y" ORDER BY created DESC`, and Jira runs it. The response then returns issues from any project, not the issues assigned to one email. An email containing a lone `"` or `\` instead yields malformed JQL and a Jira error, not a result.
severity_reason: The injection is real and reachable from request input. But the Jira request is sent without credentials, and the route already lets any caller query any assignee. `getIssue` exposes arbitrary issue keys too. So the extra exposure depends on Jira permissions configured outside the repo, and the code alone does not show an exploitable privilege escalation.

reason: The claim does not match the code. In src/store.ts:21, Store.findByName calls this.db.query with a constant SQL string that uses a `?` placeholder, and passes `name` separately in the params array ([name]). It does not concatenate or interpolate `name` into the SQL text. The Db interface (src/store.ts:4) takes the SQL and its params as separate arguments. A search of src/ found no other definition of findByName and no other SELECT query. A repository name that contains a quote is therefore passed as a bound value and cannot change the SQL statement.
severity_reason: There is no defect. The query is parameterized, so it has no SQL injection risk.

reason: In src/tasks.ts, createFixTask (line 13) builds a local `task` with `state: "running", feedback: null` (line 14), inserts it (line 15), and then writes the feedback to the store in a separate `store.update(id, { feedback })` call (line 16). That update only changes the store. It never changes the local `task` object. So `emit({ ...task })` on line 17 always sends `feedback: null`, and the returned `task` on line 18 also has null feedback. This happens on every call, not only under a race. The poll race is also plausible. The record is stored as `running` with null feedback before line 16 runs, and poll (lines 21-24) runs whatever `store.runnable()` returns. However, no TaskStore implementation exists in the repository, so I can't confirm which states runnable() includes or whether poll can see the gap between the two writes. The emit/return defect alone confirms the issue at the fix location. Nothing in the repo calls createFixTask, and I found no guard that would stop it.
failure_scenario: Call createFixTask(store, "t1", "please fix the null check", emit). The store gets {id:"t1", state:"running", feedback:null}, and then its feedback is updated. But emit receives {id:"t1", state:"running", feedback:null}, and the caller gets back a Task whose feedback is also null. Any listener or dashboard that relies on the emitted event never sees the feedback. Also, if a concurrent poll() calls store.runnable() between the insert and the update, and the store treats running tasks as runnable, run() gets the task without its feedback.
severity_reason: The emitted event and the returned value lose the feedback on every createFixTask call, not only in a rare race, so the wrong data sits on the main path for creating fix tasks. This is not a security or persistence issue, because the store does end up holding the feedback.
